item.title: authn-bridge
item.description:
People log in at their own university, through RENATER’s Fédération Éducation-Recherche or eduGAIN, and applications get an OpenID Connect token. The same login can also have an SSH key certified, an X.509 client certificate issued for NFS over TLS, an application password set for SMB and S3, or a WireGuard key registered. The provider can revoke what it issued, and it publishes signed lists of what it has revoked; an access token already handed out stays valid until it expires. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, one binary. These pages describe v0.23.4.

go install github.com/go-authn/bridge/cmd/authn-bridge@v0.23.4

authn-bridge keygen --key /var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc.key --salt /var/lib/authn-bridge/salt
authn-bridge metadata --config /etc/authn-bridge > sp.xml # register this with the federation
authn-bridge check --config /etc/authn-bridge
authn-bridge --config /etc/authn-bridge # serve

Before v0.20.0 the command was bridge. That is also iproute2’s/sbin/bridge, installed on practically every Linux system, and whichever came first on PATH won. The module path is still github.com/go-authn/bridge.

Why a bridge

A research federation speaks SAML. Its members are hundreds of identity providers, one per institution, listed in a signed metadata document the federation publishes. Applications written today want OpenID Connect, and trust one provider. authn-bridge is that one provider: a SAML service provider on one side, registered once with the federation, and an OpenID provider on the other.

A gateway decides who everybody is for every application behind it, so most of this program is refusals. It refuses metadata the federation did not sign, an assertion that names somebody from another institution’s domain, groups an IdP has no authority over, and a configuration that would let any of these through.A configuration that cannot be served safely does not start.

What it prints at startup 

$ authn-bridge --config etc/bridge-admin.hcl
admin API on unix:///tmp/authn/run/admin.sock
metrics on 127.0.0.1:28475
authn-bridge v0.23.4: http://127.0.0.1:28473 on 127.0.0.1:28473

This is a test provider on loopback (an http:// issuer is accepted only on a loopback host). It fetches the federation’s metadata before it listens. A provider that cannot name a single institution is one nobody can log in through,so without the metadata it exits rather than starts.

Where to go next

Installing it the user, the directories, the systemd unit, the keys
The configuration every block, check, and what is refused at startup
The federation side metadata, its signer’s fingerprint, scopes, and what an IdP may assert
Tokens ID tokens, access tokens, the device grant, application passwords, WireGuard keys
Resource indicators a token for one of a client’s resource servers at a time (RFC 8707)
Certificates SSH certificates, the EuroHPC profile, X.509 client certificates for NFS
Revocation the signed KRL and CRL, and the Shared Signals transmitter
The admin API disabling a person or an institution, health and metrics

The lists it signs are read by authn-revokd for a plain sshd or a TLS server, and bygo-fileshare,which checks them itself.

What it is not

  • One process. With a state block, refresh tokens and the access tokens honoured at /userinfo survive a restart. Logins in progress, codes and device grants do not. The state is written through and read at start, so two instances on one database would each miss what the other wrote.
  • No dynamic client registration, and no front- or back-channel logout.
  • No users or groups to add. People exist because their institution vouches for them, and their groups are what it asserts.

Licence

BSD-3-Clause.

item.title: Tokens, passwords and keys
item.description:
Every credential here starts with the same login at the person’s institution.What differs is who the credential is for, and how it is taken back. The certificates are on their own page.

What the provider publishes 

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .
{
"authorization_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/authorize",
"authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported": true,
"claims_parameter_supported": false,
"claims_supported": [
"sub",
"iss",
"aud",
"exp",
"iat",
"auth_time",
"nonce",
"acr",
"name",
"given_name",
"family_name",
"preferred_username",
"email",
"groups",
"eduperson_principal_name",
"eduperson_scoped_affiliation",
"eduperson_entitlement",
"entitlements",
"eduperson_assurance",
"eduperson_orcid",
"schac_home_organization",
"voperson_id"
],
"code_challenge_methods_supported": [
"S256"
],
"device_authorization_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/device_authorization",
"grant_types_supported": [
"authorization_code",
"refresh_token",
"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"
],
"id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": [
"RS256"
],
"issuer": "http://127.0.0.1:28473",
"jwks_uri": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/jwks",
"request_parameter_supported": false,
"request_uri_parameter_supported": false,
"response_modes_supported": [
"query"
],
"response_types_supported": [
"code"
],
"scopes_supported": [
"openid",
"profile",
"email",
"eduperson",
"groups"
],
"subject_types_supported": [
"public",
"pairwise"
],
"token_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/token",
"token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": [
"client_secret_basic",
"client_secret_post",
"none"
],
"userinfo_endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:28473/userinfo"
}

The authorization code flow, with PKCE S256 required for every client. A request with no code_challenge_method is refused rather than read as S256,since RFC 7636 makes plain the default. A confidential client configuredpkce = "or_nonce" may send an OpenID nonce instead.

The ID token

For the client, and about the login, not the person: RS256, aud the client ID, sub, auth_time, at_hash, the nonce when the request had one, andacr when the IdP said which authentication context it used. Lifetimeid_token_lifetime, five minutes by default.

Nothing about the person is in it. The claims the scopes release are at/userinfo, as OIDC Core 5.4 says when an access token is issued, and one always is. A client whose ID token is itself the credential, such as opkssh,sets id_token_claims = true to have them copied in. An ID token is only issued for a request with the openid scope.

scope releases
profile name, given_name, family_name, preferred_username
email email (never email_verified)
eduperson eduperson_principal_name, eduperson_scoped_affiliation, eduperson_entitlement and entitlements, eduperson_assurance, eduperson_orcid, schac_home_organization, voperson_id (the SAML subject-id, lower-cased)
groups groups

The access token

For the resource servers in the client’s audience, as RFC 9068 describes:signed with signing_key_file (RS256) or access_token_key_file (ES256),typ: at+jwt, valid token_lifetime (an hour by default). It carries what a resource server needs to decide without asking anybody: preferred_username,groups, idp (the entity ID of the IdP that vouched), scope, client_id,and session_end when the IdP said when its session ends.The groups can be left out, per client: below.

A client whose audience names several resource servers can ask for a token addressed to one of them, with RFC 8707’s resource: seeseveral resource servers.

What it leaves out, and why

No auth_time and no acr, although RFC 9068 allows both. They stay in the ID token, where OIDC Core puts them. Nothing reads them from an access token: not this provider, which looks a token up by its jti, and not go-fileshare. An access token, however, is also pasted as an SSH keyboard-interactive answer (ssh-oidc’s mccli, checked by motley-cue at/userinfo), and OpenSSH reads 1023 characters of one; an IdP’s acr alone,urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PasswordProtectedTransport, is about 90 of them. Before v0.22.0 the access token carried both.

The length of an ES256 access token (access_token_key_file) for a long eppn and three AARC entitlements, measured by authn-bridge’s TestES256AccessTokens with an issuer of a real length, against the shibmd:Scope lengths of RENATER’s metadata (743 scopes):

scope length characters
13 median 885
22 95th percentile 945
29 99th percentile 992
44 the longest 1092: over

Before v0.22.0 the same token was 1014 / 1074 / 1121 / 1221 characters: over from the 95th percentile on. What still does not fit is the longest scopes and, above all, many groups: every entitlement adds its whole URN, and nothing bounds how many an IdP sends. An RS256 access token, signed with a 3072-bit key, is about 1150 characters before any group, so a token meant for SSH is signed ES256. Past 1023 characters, mccli asks motley-cue for a one-time password instead, which motley-cue allows by default; a token pasted into plainssh has to fit.

No groups, for a client that asks (v0.23.0). Every group adds its whole URN, and nothing bounds how many an IdP sends, so no key and no signature algorithm makes a token that carries groups fit for certain. A client withaccess_token_groups = false gets access tokens without the person’s groups:

client "oidc-agent" {
 device = true
 audience = ["ssh"]
 access_token_groups = false
}

It is meant for ssh-oidc: oidc-agent gets the token, mccli pastes it as the keyboard-interactive answer, and motley-cue checks it at /userinfo and reads the groups there. Measured by authn-bridge’s TestAccessTokenWithoutGroups, an ES256 token for somebody in 50 groups, with the longest RENATER scope (44) and an issuer of a real length, is 732 characters.

Against a test federation, a person in three groups logs in through that client, with the device grant:

$ authn-bridge token --issuer http://127.0.0.1:28473 --client oidc-agent --scope "openid eduperson groups" --cache var/tokens.json > at
To log in, open http://127.0.0.1:28473/device
and enter the code ZNBP-NMXM
(or open http://127.0.0.1:28473/device?user_code=ZNBP-NMXM)
$ tr -d '\n' < at | wc -c
625

The token names the person and their IdP, and no group:

$ cut -d. -f2 at | tr "_-" "/+" | jq -R "@base64d | fromjson"
{
"aud": "ssh",
"client_id": "oidc-agent",
"exp": 1793017858,
"iat": 1793014258,
"idp": "https://idp.univ-example.example/idp/shibboleth",
"iss": "http://127.0.0.1:28473",
"jti": "T1qu1-IjIqirgQedQ6hkQCUfeM0OFANOESdXKc3yrJA",
"preferred_username": "alice@univ-example.example",
"scope": "openid eduperson groups",
"sub": "UmCstEtvM1rTavlxDxNPVw-jCNFAZhdRXU405Uz985o"
}

/userinfo still serves them, as groups (scope groups) and aseduperson_entitlement (scope eduperson):

$ { printf 'Authorization: Bearer '; cat at; } > auth.hdr
$ curl -s -H @auth.hdr http://127.0.0.1:28473/userinfo | jq .
{
"eduperson_entitlement": [
"urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique#idp.univ-example.example",
"urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique:calcul#idp.univ-example.example",
"urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:hpc-users#idp.univ-example.example"
],
"eduperson_principal_name": "alice@univ-example.example",
"entitlements": [
"urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique#idp.univ-example.example",
"urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique:calcul#idp.univ-example.example",
"urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:hpc-users#idp.univ-example.example"
],
"groups": [
"urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:hpc-users#idp.univ-example.example",
"urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique#idp.univ-example.example",
"urn:geant:univ-example.example:group:physique:calcul#idp.univ-example.example"
],
"sub": "UmCstEtvM1rTavlxDxNPVw-jCNFAZhdRXU405Uz985o",
"voperson_id": "a1b2c3@univ-example.example"
}

The default stays true. go-fileshare, like any resource server that decides from the token alone, needs the groups in it: leave them out only for a client whose tokens go to a server that reads /userinfo.

Refused with certificates. SSH and X.509 certificates take the person’s groups from the access token, so a client with access_token_groups = false and ssh_certificates or x509_certificates would issue certificates that carry none, and a server that authorizes by group would refuse the person with nothing anywhere saying why. check, like the server at startup, refuses the pair:

client "oidc-agent" {
 device = true
 audience = ["ssh"]
 access_token_groups = false
 ssh_certificates = true
}
$ authn-bridge check --config etc/bridge.hcl
authn-bridge: client "oidc-agent": access_token_groups = false with ssh_certificates or x509_certificates: the certificates take the groups from the access token, and would carry none -- use one client for the certificates and another for tokens pasted into ssh
$ echo $?
1

Give the certificates one client, and the tokens pasted into ssh another.

A token holding one of the provider’s own scopes (ssh, nfs,app_password, wireguard, wireguard_peers) is addressed to the provider alone: its aud is the issuer, and those endpoints refuse any other. A token a resource server received cannot be replayed here:

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:28473/ssh/certificate -d x -D - -o -
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Www-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Date: Mon, 26 Oct 2026 11:36:20 GMT
Content-Length: 23
the token is not valid

An access token already handed out is a signed statement a resource server checks on its own. What RevokePerson ends is everything that comes back here with it; the resource server learns from Shared Signals.

Rotating the token signing key

Every relying party verifies tokens with the keys published at /jwks. A key changed in place invalidates every token they hold, and one used before they have fetched it is refused. retired_signing_key_files makes both safe: a key listed there is published and never signs. Rotating takes two restarts, since the provider does not reload its configuration and a SIGHUP is ignored. This section is written from the bridge’s README after its pull request #80 (merged on 2026-10-26,after the v0.23.4 tag).

  1. Make the next key, beside the current one. The command refuses to overwrite a file:

    authn-bridge keygen --key /var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc-2026-10.key

  2. Publish it before it signs. Add it to retired_signing_key_files, leavesigning_key_file alone, run authn-bridge check, and restart:

    signing_key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc-2026-04.key" # still signing
retired_signing_key_files = ["/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc-2026-10.key"] # published only

    /jwks now lists both kids, and new tokens still carry the old one. Wait at least as long as the longest a relying party caches the key set. One that fetches again on an unknown kid (go-authn/oidc does, at most once per its MinRefresh)needs no wait; one that caches for a fixed time needs that time.

  3. Swap. Make the new key signing_key_file and move the old one toretired_signing_key_files. Then authn-bridge check and restart:

    signing_key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc-2026-10.key"
retired_signing_key_files = ["/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc-2026-04.key"]

    /jwks still lists both kids, and new tokens carry the new one. Tokens signed with the old key keep verifying.

  4. Retire the old key once no token it signed can still be presented: after at least the longest of token_lifetime (1 h by default) and id_token_lifetime (5 min), plus the relying parties’ clock skew and their key-set cache. For opkssh, wait the PK Token lifetime instead (a day by default, up to a week).Then remove it from the list and restart: /jwks lists one kid.

Check at each step with curl -s https://login.example.org/jwks for the kids published, and the kid of a fresh token, which is the first segment of any access or ID token, base64url-decoded.

An access_token_key_file (ES256) rotates the same way: write the next one withauthn-bridge keygen --access-token-key, and a retired one goes inretired_signing_key_files like any other. Without a state block, each restart logs everybody out, because refresh tokens and /userinfo live in memory; the access tokens already issued still verify at the resource servers.

The README reports that this was verified end to end with llmflow-gateway as the relying party, in go-llmflow/bench (e2e/oidc, TestBridge/c/key-rotation): after step 2 /jwks lists both kids while tokens still carry the old one; after step 3 a token signed before the swap and one signed after are both accepted, with a single key-set fetch; and an SSO login right after the swap works.

Without a browser: the device grant

A WebDAV client, a script, a terminal has no browser to send to a university. A client with device = true asks for a code (RFC 8628), and the person logs in on any other device:

client "rclone" {
 device = true
 audience = ["fileshare"]
 refresh_lifetime = "720h" # refresh tokens, off unless set
 name = "rclone (WebDAV)"
}

authn-bridge token --issuer https://login.example.org --client rclone prints an access token, logging in the first time and refreshing after that; it is golang.org/x/oauth2’s device client, not one written here.
user codes eight letters from BCDFGHJKLMNPQRSTVWXZ (no vowels, no digits), valid ten minutes; ten wrong codes per host in that time (an IPv4 address, an IPv6 /64), and ten times as many for the /24 or /48 around it
polling every five seconds; polling faster earns slow_down
waiting devices at most 20,000; past that the oldest is pushed out rather than everybody refused
refresh tokens rotated at every use, inside a family whose end is fixed at the login by refresh_lifetime; a retired one used again revokes the family and the access tokens it bought

Application passwords

NTLMv2 and SigV4 prove a secret the server must already hold, so no token will do for SMB or S3. A client with app_passwords = true lets a token with theapp_password scope set one, generated and shown once:authn-bridge app-password --issuer ... --client files (--remove deletes it).

app_passwords {
 driver = "sqlite" # sqlite, postgres or mysql
 dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/apppw.dsn"
 store = ["nt_hash"] # the default, SMB only; add "password" for S3
 lifetime = "2160h" # the default, 90 days
 # table = "app_passwords" # the default
}

The table is created if missing: login, password, nt_hash, expires, idp.Only what the protocols need is stored: the NT hash for SMB, the password itself only when store asks for it. go-fileshare reads it with a users "sql" block;name the columns in its query, never *.

Disabling a person removes their password; disabling an institution removes its people’s. A removed password stops working in go-fileshare when it next reads its directory.

WireGuard keys

WireGuard authenticates a peer by its public key and nothing else: no certificate, no expiry, no revocation. So the provider keeps the answer towhose is this key, and may it still connect? The device’s VPN client registers the public key, for a lease; the private key never leaves the device;a gateway reads the live keys as a list signed for it alone.

certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json" # keys are recorded beside the certificates

wireguard {
 lifetime = "24h" # the default: how long a key is listed; registering again renews it
 max_keys = 10 # the default: devices per person
}

client "vpn" { # what people log in with
 device = true
 wireguard_keys = true
}

client "vpn-gw" { # the gateway's own client
 secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/vpn-gw.secret"
 wireguard_peers = ["vpn"] # the clients whose keys it reads
 ssf_receiver = true # optional: told at once when somebody is disabled
}
POST /wireguard/key {"public_key": "...", "device": "laptop"}, with a token of the wireguard scope; answers the lease’s end
DELETE /wireguard/key {"public_key": "..."}: the owner takes a key back
GET /wireguard/peers for the gateway’s own client_credentials token, scope wireguard_peers: a signed JWT of type wireguard-peers+jwt, addressed to that gateway, valid five minutes

A key somebody else holds, a key that was taken back, and one key too many are refused with 409. A gateway client must be confidential, and must name clients that have wireguard_keys. The format of the list, and the gateway’s side, are go-authn/wireguard’s.

OpenPubkey and opkssh

opkssh turns an ID token into SSH logins with no CA at all, and the token it makes (a PK Token) outlives the ID token inside it. The provider returns thenonce verbatim in the code flow and in the device flow, signs RS256, and keeps a retired key published for as long as retired_signing_key_files names it, so that a PK Token signed before a rotation still verifies:

retired_signing_key_files = ["/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc-2026-03.key"]

Give opkssh a client of its own with id_token_claims = true: it matches people on the PK Token’s claims, and its ID token travels to every server it logs into.

item.title: Several resource servers: a token for one at a time
item.description:
A client whose audience names several resource servers, such as a portal in front of several file servers, gets access tokens addressed to all of them.Any one of those servers can then take a token it received and present it to the others: RFC 8707 §3 says this is why an audience should be restricted. Since v0.21.0 the client can ask, with RFC 8707’s resource parameter, for a token addressed to one of them. This page describes v0.23.4; what v0.22.0 did differently is at the end.

Without resource, nothing changes: the access token is for the client’s wholeaudience, as the tokens page describes.

The client

Nothing needs turning on. Every URI in the client’s audience can be asked for.The examples below use a confidential client with refresh tokens, and a device client with the same audience:

client "portal" {
 secret_file = "etc/portal.secret"
 redirect_uris = ["http://127.0.0.1:9/portal"]
 audience = ["https://fs-paris.example.org/", "https://fs-lyon.example.org/"]
 refresh_lifetime = "8h"
}

client "files-cli" {
 device = true
 audience = ["https://fs-paris.example.org/", "https://fs-lyon.example.org/"]
}
$ authn-bridge check --config etc/bridge.hcl
issuer http://127.0.0.1:28473
SAML entity http://127.0.0.1:28473/saml
tls none (a reverse proxy in front)
federation 1 IdPs, 1 usable here, valid until 2026-11-02T11:30:50Z
client portal (confidential, public subject, audience [https://fs-paris.example.org/ https://fs-lyon.example.org/])
client files-cli (public, public subject, audience [https://fs-paris.example.org/ https://fs-lyon.example.org/])

check lists the audience and says nothing more about it. In particular, it does not say which entries can be asked for: only an absolute URI without a fragment can be. A logical name such as fileshare, or a URI with a #, is accepted in audience and still goes into the token when no resource is named,but a resource naming it is refused.

A token for one server

The person logs in as usual (here, against a test federation, with the authorization request naming no resource). The client then names one server when it exchanges the code:

$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=authorization_code -d code="$(cat code)" \
-d code_verifier="$(cat verifier)" -d redirect_uri=http://127.0.0.1:9/portal \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-paris.example.org/ \
-o tokens.json -w "%{http_code}\n"
200
$ jq -r .access_token tokens.json | cut -d. -f2 | tr "_-" "/+" |
jq -R "@base64d | fromjson | {aud, client_id, scope}"
{
"aud": "https://fs-paris.example.org/",
"client_id": "portal",
"scope": "openid profile"
}

The aud is the value asked for, exactly as it was sent, and nothing else. A server that checks its audience, as go-authn/oidc does, accepts this token at Paris and refuses it at Lyon.

Another server, at the next refresh

The refresh token keeps the whole grant (RFC 8707 §2.2), so the next refresh can ask for another server:

$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token="$(jq -r .refresh_token tokens.json)" \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-lyon.example.org/ \
-o tokens.json -w "%{http_code}\n"
200
$ jq -r .access_token tokens.json | cut -d. -f2 | tr "_-" "/+" |
jq -R "@base64d | fromjson | {aud, client_id, scope}"
{
"aud": "https://fs-lyon.example.org/",
"client_id": "portal",
"scope": "openid profile"
}

The scope is the same for both servers: the provider does not reduce it per resource.

A server the client may not have

A resource that is not in the client’s audience is refused withinvalid_target:

$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token="$(jq -r .refresh_token tokens.json)" \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-nantes.example.org/ -w "\n%{http_code}\n" | jq .
{
"error": "invalid_target",
"error_description": "resource \"https://fs-nantes.example.org/\" is not one this client may ask a token for"
}
400

A refused refresh does not spend the refresh token. The request is checked before the token is used up, so the same refresh token still works. Asked for no resource, it gives a token for the client’s whole audience:

$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token="$(jq -r .refresh_token tokens.json)" \
-o tokens.json -w "%{http_code}\n"
200
$ jq -r .access_token tokens.json | cut -d. -f2 | tr "_-" "/+" |
jq -R "@base64d | fromjson | {aud, client_id, scope}"
{
"aud": [
"https://fs-paris.example.org/",
"https://fs-lyon.example.org/"
],
"client_id": "portal",
"scope": "openid profile"
}

The value is compared with the audience entries as a string, not normalised as a URI. The same server without its final / is a different resource:

$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token="$(jq -r .refresh_token tokens.json)" \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-paris.example.org \
-w "\n%{http_code}\n" | jq .
{
"error": "invalid_target",
"error_description": "resource \"https://fs-paris.example.org\" is not one this client may ask a token for"
}
400

Bounding the grant at the authorization request

resource can also be sent with the authorization request. It then bounds the grant: the code, and the refresh tokens that follow, are for that server, and a later token request can name it again but never another one. After a login whose authorization request carried resource=https://fs-paris.example.org/:

$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=authorization_code -d code="$(cat code)" \
-d code_verifier="$(cat verifier)" -d redirect_uri=http://127.0.0.1:9/portal \
-o tokens.json -w "%{http_code}\n"
200
$ jq -r .access_token tokens.json | cut -d. -f2 | tr "_-" "/+" |
jq -R "@base64d | fromjson | {aud, client_id, scope}"
{
"aud": "https://fs-paris.example.org/",
"client_id": "portal",
"scope": "openid profile"
}
$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token="$(jq -r .refresh_token tokens.json)" \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-lyon.example.org/ -w "\n%{http_code}\n" | jq .
{
"error": "invalid_target",
"error_description": "resource \"https://fs-lyon.example.org/\" was not part of the authorization"
}
400

The authorization request may carry several resource values: it is the one parameter that may be repeated there. Each is checked, a value given twice counts once, and the grant is for the servers named. After a login whose authorization request carried resource=https://fs-paris.example.org/ andresource=https://fs-lyon.example.org/, the code gives a token for both, and each refresh can ask for either:

$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=authorization_code -d code="$(cat code)" \
-d code_verifier="$(cat verifier)" -d redirect_uri=http://127.0.0.1:9/portal \
-o tokens.json -w "%{http_code}\n"
200
$ jq -r .access_token tokens.json | cut -d. -f2 | tr "_-" "/+" |
jq -R "@base64d | fromjson | {aud, client_id, scope}"
{
"aud": [
"https://fs-paris.example.org/",
"https://fs-lyon.example.org/"
],
"client_id": "portal",
"scope": "openid profile"
}
$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token="$(jq -r .refresh_token tokens.json)" \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-paris.example.org/ \
-o tokens.json -w "%{http_code}\n"
200
$ jq -r .access_token tokens.json | cut -d. -f2 | tr "_-" "/+" |
jq -R "@base64d | fromjson | {aud, client_id, scope}"
{
"aud": "https://fs-paris.example.org/",
"client_id": "portal",
"scope": "openid profile"
}
$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token="$(jq -r .refresh_token tokens.json)" \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-lyon.example.org/ \
-o tokens.json -w "%{http_code}\n"
200
$ jq -r .access_token tokens.json | cut -d. -f2 | tr "_-" "/+" |
jq -R "@base64d | fromjson | {aud, client_id, scope}"
{
"aud": "https://fs-lyon.example.org/",
"client_id": "portal",
"scope": "openid profile"
}

With a state block, the grant’s resources are stored with the refresh token,so a restart does not widen it.

A resource the client may not have is refused at the authorization endpoint too,as an error sent back to the client’s redirect URI. One such value among good ones refuses the whole request:

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{redirect_url}\n" -G http://127.0.0.1:28473/authorize \
-d response_type=code -d client_id=portal -d scope=openid -d state=s1 \
--data-urlencode redirect_uri=http://127.0.0.1:9/portal \
-d code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM -d code_challenge_method=S256 \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-paris.example.org/ \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-nantes.example.org/
302 http://127.0.0.1:9/portal?error=invalid_target&error_description=resource+%22https%3A%2F%2Ffs-nantes.example.org%2F%22+is+not+one+this+client+may+ask+a+token+for&iss=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A28473&state=s1

At the token endpoint, one resource per request. A token is for one server,for the grant’s servers, or for the whole audience; it is never for a list the token request chooses. A second resource there is refused like any repeated parameter:

$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=refresh_token -d refresh_token="$(jq -r .refresh_token tokens.json)" \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-paris.example.org/ \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-lyon.example.org/ -w "\n%{http_code}\n" | jq .
{
"error": "invalid_request",
"error_description": "resource appears more than once"
}
400

The rules

where resource is taken by the authorization endpoint, and by the token endpoint with the authorization_code and refresh_token grants
how many at the authorization endpoint, several: each is checked, and one that is refused refuses the request. At the token endpoint, one: a second is invalid_request
what may be named an absolute URI without a fragment that is, character for character, an entry of the client’s audience
the token’s aud the resource named at the token endpoint; if none, the resources the authorization request named, in the order given; if neither, the client’s whole audience
a refresh may name one of the resources the authorization request named or, if it named none, any URI of the client’s audience. The new refresh token keeps the whole grant
refused invalid_target, sent back to the redirect URI at the authorization endpoint and returned as a 400 error by the token endpoint. A refused refresh does not spend the refresh token
other grants resource with client_credentials, at the device authorization request or when polling for a device token is refused with invalid_target, not ignored: a client that asked for a token for one server must not receive one for another. A device token is always for the whole audience
the provider’s own scopes a token with ssh, nfs, app_password, wireguard or wireguard_peers is for the provider alone, and only the issuer itself may be named

The refusal of other grants, at the token endpoint and at the device authorization request:

$ curl -s --netrc-file etc/portal.netrc http://127.0.0.1:28473/token \
-d grant_type=client_credentials \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-paris.example.org/ -w "\n%{http_code}\n" | jq .
{
"error": "invalid_target",
"error_description": "resource indicators are taken with the authorization_code and refresh_token grants"
}
400
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28473/device_authorization -d client_id=files-cli \
--data-urlencode resource=https://fs-paris.example.org/ -w "\n%{http_code}\n" | jq .
{
"error": "invalid_target",
"error_description": "resource indicators are taken with the authorization_code and refresh_token grants"
}
400

Where this departs from RFC 8707

RFC 8707 authn-bridge v0.23.4
§2: “Multiple resource parameters MAY be used” at the authorization endpoint, as written. At the token endpoint, one: a second resource is invalid_request, which §3 allows (“an authorization server may be unwilling or unable to fulfill a token request with multiple resources”)
§2.2: the parameter applies “for all grant types” only authorization_code and refresh_token. With client_credentials or the device grant it is refused with invalid_target, at the device authorization request as when polling
§2: the value “SHOULD NOT include a query component” not checked. What is checked is that the value is absolute, has no fragment, and is in the client’s audience
§2: the server “may map from that value to a more general URI or abstract identifier” no mapping: aud is the value asked for, compared with audience as a string
§2.2: “the authorization server should downscope the scope value” for each resource not done: the scope is the grant’s, whichever server is named
§2.1: a request without resource MAY be processed “by using a predefined default resource value” the default is the client’s whole audience
§2.2: a refresh may be limited “to those [resources] that were originally granted”, and the refresh token “is bound to the full original grant” as written

Before v0.22.1, v0.22.0 refused a repeated resource at the authorization endpoint with an error page, as it refuses any other repeated parameter, so a grant could not name two servers; and its device authorization request did not read resource, so a device that asked for one server got a token for the wholeaudience.

item.title: A token at the bind, in a field that is not the password
item.description:
go-authn/oidc verifies a token into an identity. The obvious way to carry one to an LDAP server is the password field, and it works once and then stops: the password field is where themfa block takes the code off the end, and a token cannot be both.

So the token goes where the protocol has a place for it. A SASL bind’s credentials are an octet string of the mechanism’s own shape, and RFC 7628’sOAUTHBEARER shape is a GS2 header followed by key/value pairs, one of which is auth=Bearer <token>:

n,,^Aauth=Bearer eyJ…^A^A

The password field is left alone. On one listener, at the same time, a person can type a password with a code on the end and another can send a token.

oidc {
 issuer = "https://login.example.org/realms/staff" # the "iss" a token must carry, and where discovery starts
 audience = "ldap" # this server's client id at the provider

 # username_claim = "preferred_username" which claim names the person here
 # jwks_url = "…" skips discovery, for a provider that does not publish it
 # allow_plaintext = true only when TLS is terminated in front of this process
}

issuer and audience are required. Without username_claim, the name ispreferred_username, then email when email_verified is true, then sub.With the block, the root DSE advertises the mechanism:

$ ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -s base -b '' supportedSASLMechanisms
dn:
supportedSASLMechanisms: OAUTHBEARER

Without it, every SASL bind is answered authMethodNotSupported — not this way, which sends a client somewhere different from wrong password.

Discovery happens at startup

The provider’s discovery document and keys are read when the server starts,and by check. A provider that cannot be reached stops the server where somebody is watching, rather than refusing every bind later:

$ authnd check cases/oidc.hcl
authnd: oidc "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff": oidc: reading https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration: Get "https://127.0.0.1:1/realms/staff/.well-known/openid-configuration": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused

An issuer that is not https is refused, except on loopback:

$ authnd check cases/oidc-http.hcl
authnd: oidc "http://login.example.org/realms/staff": oidc: http://login.example.org/realms/staff is not https: the key set decides every signature, and over cleartext so does anybody on the way

How many factors is a token?

Whatever the issuer says it checked, and nothing more. A token carries RFC 8176’s amr, the methods the provider used. That is the only evidence there is, so it is what the mfa policy counts, by kind:

amr method kind
pwd, pin, kba, mca knowledge
otp, hwk, swk, sms, tel, sc, pop, user, wia, mfa possession
fpt, face, iris, retina, vbm, geo inherence
anything else unknown, which never satisfies distinct_kinds
no amr at all one factor, possession — the token itself

Two methods of one kind are one factor. The alternative would be this server inventing a second factor nobody performed; and a server that believes the issuer about who this is has no separate ground for disbelieving it abouthow it checked.

With an mfa block, check says it:

$ authnd check sasl
ldaps://127.0.0.1:3636, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS WITH
alice the configuration file a password account, uidObject uid
tess the configuration file a password and a one-time-code secret account, uidObject uid
alice has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
tess has no uidNumber, gidNumber or homeDirectory: not a posixAccount, published as account, uidObject
a bind carries a password with a 6-digit code after it, of two different kinds
or a token from http://127.0.0.1:18481, over SASL OAUTHBEARER over TLS
a token counts for the factors its amr claim names, so one with no amr is refused by this policy
alice has no second factor here, so a password cannot satisfy this policy; a token whose amr names two kinds still can
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

alice has no totp_secret, so a password with a code can never be enough for them; a token whose amr names two kinds can, as the first bind below shows.

What the binds look like

The issuer here is a small test provider on loopback, and oidctool a test client written for these pages: it signs a token for the name given, with the amr given, sends it in an OAUTHBEARER bind (with an authzid when a fifth argument names one), and prints the bind’s result code and the server’s SASL credentials. These transcripts, and the server lines below, were printed by the v0.10.0 release binary and not run again, since oidctool is part of no release. Against the configuration above, over ldaps://:

$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 0, serverSaslCreds
$ ./oidctool alice '' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 49
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","kba"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 49
$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls tess
bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"insufficient_scope","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"}
$ ./oidctool zed '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3636 tls
bind result 14, serverSaslCreds {"status":"invalid_token","openid-configuration":"http://127.0.0.1:18481/.well-known/openid-configuration"}

0 is success, 49 invalidCredentials, 14 saslBindInProgress. A["pwd","kba"] token names two methods of one kind, so it counts once. And to the same configuration without cert_file and key_file, on a plaintext listener:

$ ./oidctool alice '["pwd","otp"]' 127.0.0.1:3893 clear
bind result 13

13 is confidentialityRequired: a token is not taken over a connection that is not encrypted.

What the server wrote for the four binds over ldaps:// that were refused:

alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered
alice was refused: mfa: the policy needs 2 factor(s) and 1 were offered
alice was refused: the token is for "alice" and asks to act as "tess"; this server does not delegate
zed was refused: the token verified, and no source here publishes anybody by that name

and for the plaintext one:

a token was refused: OAUTHBEARER was offered over a connection that is not encrypted, and allow_plaintext is not set

A successful OAUTHBEARER bind leaves the connection bound asuid=<name>,ou=people,<base_dn>, spelled as every other entry is.

What it refuses

  • A token in the clear. A bearer token needs no other half: whoever reads it off the wire is that person until it expires. allow_plaintext = true exists for a deployment that terminates TLS in front of this process, andcheck then says a token may cross this socket in the clear.
  • A request to be somebody else. The GS2 header may name an authzid. A token for alice carrying a request to act as tess is refused, not quietly treated as either.
  • A token for somebody no source here publishes. The client is told onlyinvalid_token; which names exist is not something to hand out one guess at a time. The reason is in the server’s output.
  • Channel binding. A GS2 header with p= — the client insists on channel binding — is refused: this server does not do it, and accepting the header while binding nothing would let the client believe the channel was checked.
  • A mechanism this server does not speak, with authMethodNotSupported.

A refusal of the token itself is RFC 7628 §3.2.3’s: a JSON error carryingopenid-configuration, returned as saslBindInProgress so the client can send the ^A that ends the exchange. A token that verifies but does not satisfy the mfa policy is answered plainly invalidCredentials, as the second and third binds above show.

A token does not set a password

A person who has only ever signed in with a token cannot use that session to give themselves a first password, and a person who has one must still send it to change it. See changing a password.

item.title: oidc — verifying a bearer token
item.description:
Who does this bearer token say is asking, and should it be believed? Discovery, the key set, and the checks a resource server must make — in pure Go, with no dependencies outside the standard library.

go get github.com/go-authn/oidc@v0.4.1

There is no login flow here: no redirect, no code exchange, no client secret,no cookies. This is the resource-server half — something arrives with a token, and this says who that is.

Example 

package main

import (
 "context"
 "fmt"
 "log"
 "net/http"
 "strings"

 "github.com/go-authn/oidc"
)

func main() {
 // Discovery happens here, at startup: an issuer that does not answer is
 // a server that cannot authenticate anybody.
 v, err := oidc.New(context.Background(), oidc.Config{
 Issuer: "https://login.example.org",
 Audience: "fileshare",
 Type: "at+jwt", // a resource server takes access tokens, not ID tokens
 })
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }

 http.HandleFunc("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
 raw, ok := strings.CutPrefix(r.Header.Get("Authorization"), "Bearer ")
 if !ok {
 http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
 return
 }
 tok, err := v.Verify(r.Context(), raw)
 if err != nil {
 log.Print(err) // which check refused it: for this log only
 http.Error(w, "unauthorized", http.StatusUnauthorized)
 return
 }
 fmt.Fprintln(w, tok.Subject(), tok.Username(), tok.Groups())
 })
 log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

A Verifier is safe for concurrent use and holds the key set: build one at startup and keep it. Verify’s error says which check refused the token, for the server’s log; the client gets one refusal whatever the check.

Three configurations New refuses before anything is fetched:

package main

import (
 "context"
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/oidc"
)

func main() {
 ctx := context.Background()
 for _, cfg := range []oidc.Config{
 {Issuer: "http://login.example.org", Audience: "fileshare"},
 {Issuer: "https://login.example.org"},
 {Audience: "fileshare"},
 } {
 _, err := oidc.New(ctx, cfg)
 fmt.Println(err)
 }
}
oidc: http://login.example.org is not https: the key set decides every signature, and over cleartext so does anybody on the way
oidc: no audience: a token minted for another service is a valid token, and a verifier that does not check accepts every one the issuer ever signed
oidc: no issuer: a verifier without one accepts tokens from anybody

The rest of Config is optional: JWKSURL skips discovery; UsernameClaim and GroupsClaim (default groups) name the claims; ClockSkew andMinRefresh default to one minute; Client is the HTTP client, for a proxy,a private CA or a timeout. A Token reads Subject, Issuer, Audience,Email, EmailVerified, Username, Groups, Expiry, NotBefore andIssuedAt; Claim(name, &v) decodes any other claim, and Has(name) says whether it is there.

What it accepts

Ten signature algorithms, as an allowlist: RS256 RS384 RS512,PS256 PS384 PS512, ES256 ES384 ES512, and EdDSA (Ed25519). A token whose alg is not one of these is refused before any key is fetched.alg: none and the HMAC family are refused by not being on the list, and the key must be of the algorithm’s kind: a token claiming RS256 is checked with an RSA key or refused.

What it refuses, and why

why
alg: none a token that says it is unsigned is a JSON object somebody typed
HMAC against a public key HS256 takes a shared secret, and the issuer’s key is public: anybody could mint a token
an issuer that merely starts with the right one iss is compared whole: https://login.example.org.evil.test starts with the right string
a missing or wrong audience a token minted for another service is valid; it is not addressed to this one
a token with no expiry it is a password somebody can copy once
an issuer, a key set, or a redirect over cleartext HTTP, except to loopback the key set decides every signature
an RSA key under 2048 bits, or with n or e not in shortest form; an EC point not on its curve signatures under a short key can be forged; before v0.2.2, a 1024-bit modulus padded with zero bytes passed as 2048 bits
a key published with use other than sig a key set legitimately holds encryption keys too
with Type set, a token of another typ; with it unset, a typ other than JWT or at+jwt (a token with no typ header passes) RFC 9068 §4: a resource server checks typ: at+jwt, or it takes an ID token for an access token whenever the audiences agree
a part that is not canonical base64url a token verifies as one string

ECDSA’s s and n − s both verify, as the algorithm allows. So a denylist or a replay cache keys on jti or sub, never on the token as sent.

Keys rotate, and an unknown key is not a way to hammer the issuer. A signature nothing held can verify is worth one refetch of the key set perMinRefresh, whether the kid is new or the same kid carries a new key.Tokens that need the key set while a fetch is under way wait for it, and a fetch that fails still counts.

Which name Username() gives. By default preferred_username, thenemail only when email_verified is true, then sub. An unverified email is a string the person typed (OIDC Core §5.1). A configured UsernameClaim is read as named, with no fallback.

What it is checked against

pyjwt signs every token in the test suite, so the verifier is never judged by a signer from the same hands. The HMAC-confusion token is forged by hand,because pyjwt refuses to produce it. testdata/fixed.json — tokens pyjwt signed once with a fixed key — lets the architecture lanes, s390x included,verify real signatures with the clock fixed. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane install pyjwt and set OIDC_REQUIRE_JUDGE, so a missing pyjwt fails rather than skips. Accepting HMAC, comparing the issuer by prefix and skipping the audience check were each tried on purpose, and each turns a test red. The coverage lane’s floor is 90%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/oidc@v0.4.1
